c.tagline: Europe's last divided capital, ringed by Venetian walls.

taxi.fareNote: Urban rides are metered; intercity or airport transfers are typically negotiated as a fixed fare in advance.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number and works island-wide; 199 is the traditional local alternative. Both reach police, fire and ambulance dispatch.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: Nicosia's atmospheric historic core inside the Venetian Walls, packed with restored Ottoman/Venetian-era houses, craft shops and tavernas just steps from the Ledra Street crossing into North Nicosia; best for first-time visitors who want to walk everywhere.

The modern commercial heart around Eleftheria Square and Makariou Avenue, lined with banks, shops and mid-range hotels right at the edge of the old walls; convenient for business, shopping, and easy access to both old and new Nicosia.

A leafy, affluent embassy and corporate district northwest of downtown, home to the city's flagship international hotel and modern apartment-hotels; suits business travelers and anyone wanting quiet, car-friendly comfort a short drive from the center.

A quieter residential quarter near the Presidential Palace, state museums/galleries and the original University of Cyprus campus; a good middle ground for travelers who want proximity to government and cultural institutions away from downtown bustle.

Nicosia's largest and most modern suburb, home to malls, the GSP stadium and mid-range apartment-hotels; best for travelers who prioritize value, parking and easy ring-road access over old-town charm.

water.note: Tap water meets EU standards and is safe to drink, though its mineral taste leads many to prefer bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid with the reloadable island-wide Motion smart card (tap on boarding), sold and topped up at kiosks and bus offices, or with a cash single-ride ticket bought directly from the driver in exact change. Tourists can also buy multi-day travel cards.
transit.hours: Urban buses generally operate about 5:30am-8pm (some routes to ~11pm), with reduced frequency on Sundays and public holidays; there is no dedicated night-bus network.
transit.note: Nicosia has no metro, tram or rail system - it is served entirely by buses, supplemented by taxis, Bolt, and walking within the compact center.

bus: Intercity coaches to Limassol, Larnaca and Paphos

transit.m: Kapnos Airport Shuttle intercity bus (~50-60 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving 5-10% in restaurants is appreciated, service is rarely pre-included, and taxi drivers don't expect a tip.

train.note: There are no railways in Cyprus. The last Cyprus Government Railway train pulled out of Nicosia at 14:57 on 31 December 1951 and reached Famagusta that afternoon, after which the line was dismantled; the old station area is now built over. Nothing has replaced it, so all intercity travel is by road, and the only rail heritage on the island is the museum at Evrychou.

bus.note: Intercity Buses (https://www.intercity-buses.com/) runs from the Solomos Square area to Limassol (about 1 hr), Larnaca (about 45 min), Paphos (about 2 hrs) and Ayia Napa, while city and district routes use the Motion smartcard and the Solomos and Constanza Bastion stands. No coach crosses an international border, because Cyprus's only land boundary is the UN buffer zone: you cross on foot at Ledra Street in the middle of the old town, or by car at Ledra Palace and Agios Dometios, showing a passport or ID at both checkpoints. On the northern side, buses from the Lefkosa (North Nicosia) terminal run to Kyrenia in about 30 minutes and Famagusta in about an hour.

ferry.note: Nicosia is the only capital on the island set well inland, roughly 50 km from the coast, so it has no port and no ferry of its own. The nearest sailings are from Kyrenia, about 25 km north through a buffer-zone crossing, where Akgunler (https://www.akgunlerbilet.com/) runs the 2.5-hour fast ferry to Tasucu in Turkey; Famagusta has a cargo link to Mersin. The government-controlled ports of Limassol (about 85 km) and Larnaca (about 50 km) currently handle cruise and cargo traffic only, with no scheduled passenger ferry to Greece.
